Name: Leah
Transcript: Thanks for doing this. There are no right or wrong answers, it's your experience I'm interested in, and we can stop whenever you like. So, to start. Can you tell me how you came to be working from home, and what it's like for you now?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: So I'm a bit different, I think, from most of the people you'll talk to. I'm a translator, Welsh and English, freelance. Mostly public sector, council documents, health board leaflets, the odd novel if I'm lucky. And I've worked from home since 2012, when Elin was born. I was at an agency in Cardiff before that, in an office, and I left to go freelance so I could be home with her. So when the pandemic came, for me nothing changed. Except that suddenly everybody else was at home too. And that changed quite a lot, actually.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What changed, when everybody else was at home?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: People understood, for the first time. For eight years, people thought I didn't really work. Friends would ring at eleven in the morning for a chat. My dad would say, now you're not busy, could you. And I'd say, Dad, I'm working, and he'd say, yes, yes, but you're at home. And then in 2020 everyone found out what it's like. And I'll be honest, there was a little bit of me that thought, well, now you know. It was quite nice to be understood.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Can you take me through a normal working day, from when you get up?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: Up at seven, Elin up, breakfast, she gets the bus to school now, she's fourteen. And then at half eight I do my walk. I put my shoes on, proper shoes, not slippers, and I walk down to the postbox at the end of the road and back. Whether I've got a letter or not. I've done it for fourteen years. And when I come back in, I'm at work. I work till twelve, I have lunch, and I work till three, and then on Mondays and Thursdays I go round to my dad's, he's got early dementia, he's on his own, and I check he's eaten and his pills. And then home, and I'll do another hour or two in the evening if a deadline's on.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What's it like, going round to your dad's in the middle of a working day?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: I take my phone. Always. And if an email comes in while I'm doing his pills, I answer it there and then, in his kitchen. Because if a client emails and I don't answer for two hours, I worry they'll think, oh, she's not really working, she's a mum at home. Which I am. But I'm also the best Welsh translator they've got for health. So I answer quickly to prove it, I suppose. A client asked me once, on a call, where are you, it sounds like there's a kettle. And there was. Dad's kettle. I said I was working from a different room today. Which was true, in a way.

Name: Leah
Transcript: The walk to the postbox. Can you tell me more about that?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: It was the first thing I worked out, when I went freelance. In the office I had a bus, a door, a desk. At home, there's nothing to tell you it's started. So I made something. The postbox is my office door. And the shoes are important. In slippers I'm at home. In shoes I'm at work. Elin knows. If she comes in and I've got my shoes on, she whispers.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Where in your home do you work? What's that space like for you?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: It's a two-bed flat, ground floor. And I work in the corner of the living room, by the window. I've got a little desk and a bookcase with my dictionaries. And for years that was fine. But I've learnt that at the end of the day, it has to go. So I have a box. A big plastic box, the kind you'd put Christmas decorations in. And at the end of the day, the laptop goes in the box, the notepad, the headphones, the dictionary I'm using. And the box goes in the cupboard under the stairs. Well, the cupboard in the hall, we haven't got stairs. And then the corner's just a corner again, with a desk in it.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What's it like, when the box goes in the cupboard?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: Like the work's gone to bed. It sounds silly. But if I can see it, I'll think about it. A word I wasn't sure of. And then I'll get up and check it, and then it's ten o'clock. So the box goes in the cupboard. It's for my own good.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What happens at the start and the end of your working day?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: The postbox and the box. I've just told you, haven't I. Started is the postbox. Finished is the box going in the cupboard. And the shoes come off. I'm quite strict about it. You have to be, when you're freelance, because nobody else will be. Nobody tells you to stop. And the clients are all over the place now, since everyone went home. Before, the council would email in office hours. Now I get an email at nine at night that says, any chance of this by the morning. And I'm a freelancer, so if I say no, they'll find someone who says yes. So sometimes the box comes back out.

Name: Leah
Transcript: How has working from home changed things with the people you live with, or the people around you?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: With Elin, it's been good. I've been there. I've been at every assembly, every sports day. That's why I did it. With my dad, it's, that's harder. My brother lives in Swansea, he works in an office, and when Dad started getting worse, it was just understood that it would be me. Because I'm at home. Because I'm flexible. That's the word. Ffion's flexible. And I am, but flexible doesn't mean I'm not working. I can go round on a Monday afternoon, but then I'm working on a Monday night to make up the hours. Nobody sees that bit.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Nobody sees that bit.

Name: Ffion
Transcript: No. It happens after Elin's in bed, at the desk, with the box out. My brother rings on a Sunday and says, how's Dad, and I tell him, and he says, I don't know how you do it. And I want to say, you could find out. But I don't.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Can you tell me about a day working from home that has stayed with you?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: There was a day in the summer holidays, Elin was home, and I had a huge job for the health board, a deadline at five. And Dad rang at two, very confused, he couldn't find his keys and he thought someone had been in the house. So I had to go. I took Elin with me. And I was sat in my dad's kitchen with the laptop on my knee, translating a leaflet about memory clinics, while he looked for his keys, and Elin looked for them with him. And I remember thinking, this is my whole life, in one room. And it was quite, I don't know. I didn't know whether to laugh or cry. I did the leaflet. We found the keys. They were in the fridge.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What, if anything, do you miss about working somewhere else? And what would you miss if you had to go back?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: I don't miss the agency. I really don't. It was all very, you had to be seen. You had to be at your desk when the boss walked past. You had to go to the drinks. I'm not good at that. At home I can just be good at the work, and the work speaks for itself. I miss colleagues, a bit. Someone to ask about a word. I've got a WhatsApp group with three other translators now, and that's my staffroom. We've never met, two of them. One's in Bangor and one's in Patagonia, actually, which is a long story. But we ask each other about words, and we moan about clients, and that's enough. That's all I ever wanted from an office, really, and I get it on my phone. And going back? I couldn't. Not with Dad. Not now. I don't think there's an office in the world that would have me on those hours.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Is there anything about working from home that we haven't touched on, that matters to you?

Name: Ffion
Transcript: Just that it's a skill. People think it's easy, you just stay in. But keeping the work in its corner, and keeping the home out of the work, that's a skill I had to learn, and I'm still learning it. It took me ten years to get to the box.
